title: Not in Kashi: God Beside You
hookLine: Kabir leaves holy Kashi to die in Maghar. where does he think God is?
carry: the lord lives in the heart, nearer than searching
tomorrow: a Sufi's tomb, and a Hindu family at the gate. why?

cards: Kashi, Benares, is the city where many Hindus hope to die: tradition says death there brings liberation. Kabir lived there nearly all his life.

Then, old, he left for Maghar, a town where, people said, dying brought a bad rebirth. A song of his in the Sikh scripture gives the reason, in paraphrase: if Kabir dies in Kashi, what credit is that to Ram?
He'd needled the mosque too, the caller shouting from the top as if God were deaf, and the temple: if worshipping a stone brought God, I'd worship a mountain. So where does he think God is?

teach.b: In one song, which Tagore put into English, God speaks. In paraphrase: where are you looking for me? I'm right beside you.
Not in temple, not in mosque. Not in the Kaaba, not on Kailash. Not in rites, not in yoga and renunciation.
Each place has a twin, and he walks past both, toward something nearer. Hindus have a name for the one that near: the antaryamin, the inner ruler of the Upanishads.

The Gita says it plainly, in paraphrase: the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. Kabir's needle isn't a ruling on anyone's worship, and the people he needled kept his songs anyway. Now a neighbor.
The Qur'an says something close, in God's own voice.
In Pickthall's translation of the fiftieth surah: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."

teach.h: NEITHER HAS TO BECOME THE OTHER.
teach.b: That's what the two share: neither puts God far off, at the end of a long trip. And an honest difference.
In the Qur'an, the one who is near is the Creator, and the creature stays a creature; Islam gives God no image and no partner. Hindus hear Kabir in other frames.
Some, reading the Upanishads, hear the one within as the deepest self. And Hindu devotion makes room for God in sacred images, the very thing Kabir needled. One nearness, two houses.

how: Hindus speak of the Lord in the heart of every being (Gita 18.61) and meditate on God within; Kabir's songs that needle both temple and mosque are sung in Hindu settings; Muslims recite the Qur'an's verse on God's nearness (50:16) in their own frame.

o: pilgrims who walked from Mecca to Mount Kailash
poets who wrote only for the royal courts of Delhi
holy people both Hindus and Muslims remember as their own

games.q: where to look. tap the pairs.
p: where Kabir chose to die, instead of Kashi
the Qur'an's picture of God's nearness
the inner ruler, God in the heart

s: Kabir left Kashi so he could die somewhere holier
he went to Maghar, said to bring a bad rebirth: God is not bought by a place.
the Qur'an says God is nearer than the jugular vein
surah 50, in Pickthall's words: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.
sharing the idea of God's nearness means the two religions teach the same thing
the nearness is shared; ideas about images, and about God and the self, differ.

games.q: after hearing your Kabir song, a Muslim friend quotes the jugular-vein verse and asks: so we believe the same thing? what's the honest answer?
o: we share the nearness; we differ on images, and on God and the self.
yes, exactly the same; only the words come from different places.
no, nothing alike; the Qur'an and Kabir disagree about everything.
games.why: Both put God near, closer than searching. The Qur'an keeps Creator and creature distinct, with no image; Hindu frames include sacred images and, for some, the deepest self.

practice: Rest a hand on your chest, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Many Hindus meditate on God seated in the heart. If you pray, say the name you use for God once, quietly, and let it rest under your hand.
If you don't, rest your attention on the breath there. When the mind runs off searching, bring it back to here, as near as you can get. Nothing to find out there.

wordCard.voice: Hindu-Muslim shared saints. Here, Kabir walking past temple and mosque alike, toward the one right beside you.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: Kailash, the Himalayan mountain of Shiva; Kabir pairs it with the Kaaba.

carryVoice: For the road: the Lord lives in the heart, nearer than any searching. Two houses name that nearness in their own words. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, a verse of Kabir (Raag Gauri): if Kabir leaves the body at Kashi, what credit is that to Ram?; the story of his death at Maghar as told in hagiographies
Couplets credited to Kabir: the mosque of piled-up stones and the call (has God gone deaf?); if worshipping a stone brought God, I'd worship a mountain
Songs of Kabir (tr. Rabindranath Tagore, 1915), poem I (where dost thou seek me? I am beside thee; not in temple nor mosque, not in Kaaba nor Kailash, not in rites, yoga or renunciation)

sources.q: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.61 (the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7 (the antaryamin, the inner ruler)
